title: Count Three-Letter Windows With No Repeats
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Slide a window of exactly 3 consecutive characters across it, one position at a time.

Return how many window positions hold three different letters. Equal windows at different positions are counted separately. A string shorter than 3 has no windows.

examples.why: The windows are "xyz", "yzz", "zzy", "zyx". Only the first and the last have no repeated letter.
"abc", "bca", "cab", "abc" all qualify. "abc" shows up twice and counts twice: this is not a count of distinct substrings.
Every window ("aab", "aba", "baa") repeats an a, even when the repeats are not next to each other.

constraints: s has only lowercase English letters
hints: How many windows are there in a string of length n?
Three letters are all different exactly when no two of the three pairs are equal. Check each window directly.
For a general window size k, keep letter counts and the number of letters seen more than once as the window slides; for k = 3, three comparisons are enough.

explain.intuition:
There are n − 2 windows. For each one you only need to know whether any letter repeats. With three letters a, b, c that means checking a ≠ b, b ≠ c and a ≠ c. The last check is the one people forget: in "aba" the repeats are not neighbors.

For a bigger window the same idea becomes a real sliding window: keep a count per letter, add the letter that enters, remove the letter that leaves, and track how many letters currently appear twice or more. It is the same bookkeeping a rate limiter does over the last k requests.
steps: For each start i from 0 to n − 3, look at s[i], s[i+1], s[i+2].
Count the window if all three pairs differ.
pitfalls: Only comparing neighbors, which counts "aba" as clean.
Counting distinct good substrings with a set instead of window positions; "abcabc" must give 4, not 3.
Looping to n − 2 inclusive and reading past the end.

solutions.title: Build a set per window
solutions.idea: Put each window's three letters in a set; the window is good when the set has size 3.

solutions.title: Sliding window with letter counts
solutions.idea: Works for any window size: keep counts and the number of letters that appear more than once inside the window.

followups: Make the window size a parameter k. What stays O(n) and what does not?
Return the number of distinct good windows instead of positions.
lcTitle: Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters
